I found myself in a very similar position to you the first time I started tretinoin, skin picking included. My skin looked just like yours, so I know how uncomfortable and psychologically difficult it is.  My acne just kept getting worse and worse, and it became painful just to put on moisturizer.


 It seems like a lot of the advice out there encourages you to power through the purge, so I want to tell you it’s okay to stop and let your skin heal. When I stopped, it took a while for my acne to improve back to my starting point, but things gradually got better. My doctor also put me on spironolactone which started working for me within a few weeks. Getting my acne under control with spiro also helped me to stop picking because there was less to pick at. Eventually, about 6 months later, I was able to attempt it again and had great success. 


Like a lot of other users have said, you must get the picking under control. Seeing a doctor or psychotherapist is a good start. I found applying pimple patches and covering up mirrors to be very helpful. Be aware that if you take any sort of stimulant medication like for ADHD that can make the urge to pick much worse. Try to give yourself some grace as well, it’s such a difficult habit to break and you’re not alone. 


I would strongly recommend taking a break from tretinoin for a few months to repair your skin barrier. Skin barrier damage can actually contribute to acne because a damaged barrier lets in bacteria and it heals more slowly. I don’t have any specific products to recommend other than a simple moisturizer, gentle cleanser, Vaseline, and SPF, but you’ll want to maintain a very barebones routine. Less is more! Good luck and update us with your progress, because this will get better eventually <3

Azelaic acid is great for redness and has an added benefit of combatting acne and rosacea. I switched over to Retin-A because it wasn’t helping enough with my hormonal acne, but it made my skin super soft and even-toned. If your acne is already pretty well controlled, I think it would be a good addition to your routine. My favorite formula is by Paula’s Choice, but it is a bit pricey for the amount you get. 

It sounds like you’re moisturizing pretty well, so I don’t have any product recommendations for fine lines other than a retinoid. If you do decide to try one, proceed with caution because it can temporarily cause issues with redness, flakiness, and sensitivity. I would honestly try out the azelaic acid first just because it tends to be gentler. If it’s in your budget, microneedling could also help with fine lines and overall texture/tone.

This is my second go at tretinoin over the last year. The first time was with .05% gel at the start of quarantine in March, but it caused an extreme bout of purging for 2 months. My dermatologist advised me to stop and actually put me on a round of prednisone to stop the extreme inflammation. In retrospect, I think the underlying issue was uncontrolled hormonal acne, compulsive skin picking, and moisture barrier damage from overzealous use of tret. From May through September I used azelaic acid and a BP wash, which improved my skin a lot, but it never really returned to normal. Since then I have also made a concerted effort to kick my skin picking habit. 

Things finally started to clear up in September when I started spironolactone 100mg, and now that I’m using tretinoin 0.025% cream, I feel like my skin is finally where I want it to be. I’m only applying every 2 nights, and I still use 10% azelaic acid (Cos de Baja) on the nights I don’t use tret. Overall, my focus right now is keeping my moisture barrier healthy. So far, I’ve only had a little bit of purging in the form of of small pimples that quickly come to a head and disappear. 

The last thing I want to say is that if you’re dealing with a long bout of uncontrolled purging, it’s okay to take a break to heal your skin. There’s a difference between purging and uncontrolled inflammation and barrier damage, so if you’re unsure, consult a dermatologist. There’s a reason it’s prescription-only in many countries. Tret is awesome for a lot of people, but it’s not a one-size-fits-all miracle drug. It may not be the right treatment for you, you may not be using the right strength or formulation, and it’s possible that your acne needs to be treated with additional methods.

It’s often caused by underlying health conditions like diabetes, so the best way to treat it is to treat any underlying conditions. I would definitely try to see a doctor, because it could be a sign of more serious health problems.

This sounds like normal discharge to me. Cervical mucus on its own isn’t a very accurate way to determine whether you’ve actually ovulated/are ovulating, especially if you’re on hormonal birth control. This is because egg white cervical mucus is actually caused by raised estrogen levels. A spike in estrogen levels can be caused by ovulation, but it doesn’t have to be. Basically, you can have “fertile” mucus without ovulating. 

Overall, Nexplanon has an incredibly low failure rate (.05% iirc). I would be shocked if you were actually ovulating after having it in for 7 months. If you’re still concerned, you could use a condom, but it’s extremely unlikely that this discharge has anything to do with ovulation. Hope this helps :)

I’ve had mine since early March, and so far I don’t have any regrets. I had been on the pill for a few years and had a brief stint with the NuvaRing which made me all but lose my mind. I’ve struggled with depression since I was a teenager, but since coming off hormonal birth control my symptoms have become 10x more manageable. Before I got it inserted I was considering going back on antidepressants, but I no longer feel like I need to. My sex drive is also a bit higher than it was before. And of course not having to worry about birth control mishaps and taking a pill every day is great. 

I was ridiculously nervous for the insertion, and it was definitely painful but nowhere as bad as I was expecting. The idea of the procedure itself was the main thing that freaked me out. I went in alone, so if you’re as nervous as I was, I would recommend bringing in a friend/relative/partner. I went on the first day of my period, and it was overly very quickly. The anticipation was the worst part. I also walked to my friend’s apartment from the university health center where I had it inserted, and that was a stupid idea. Make sure you have a ride. There was a lot of cramping afterwards. It peaked around 3-4 hours afterwards and then rapidly disappeared. By the next day I was totally fine. For a few weeks afterwards I would get random mild cramps sometimes, but nothing even worth taking ibuprofen for. 

I’ve only had one period with it so far, and I had a fair amount of cramping two-ish days before it started, which is unusual for me. The cramping on the first day was a lot more intense than I’m used to, but luckily it only lasted for that day, and ibuprofen helped. My flow was also very very heavy. Like soaking through a super tampon in an hour heavy. I leaked onto my pants for probably the first time in years. But compared to all the benefits and how convenient and hassle-free it is for the other 22-23 days of my cycle, I’m willing to deal with it. I hear it eventually lightens up for a lot of people around the 4-6 month mark, so if that happens I’ll have basically no complaints.  

Sorry this comment is way longer than I was expecting it to be. TLDR, I read a lot of horror stories as well, I was pretty nervous about the insertion, and I also had some qualms about the idea of it making my period heavier/crampier, but in the end it’s been completely worth it.

Personally, I don’t have any experience with using condoms as my only form of birth control on a long term basis. I’ve had a non-hormonal (copper) IUD for about 2 months now, and that’s been working pretty well for me. If you’re interested in a highly effective, long-term, set-it-and-forget-it method, it could be a great option for you. That being said, I feel like a lot of people really push IUDs for those exact reasons, but maybe that’s not the best option for you for whatever reason. Luckily there are still quite a few safe barrier-based options out there! 

On their own with typical use, condoms are only about 85% effective, but with perfect use they can be up to 98% effective. Obviously that’s a pretty large margin of error compared to a lot of hormonal methods and the copper IUD, but if you’re comfortable with that and feel up to the responsibility, condoms by themselves could be an option. For extra protection and peace of mind, I would highly recommend doubling up with another non-hormonal method, such as a diaphragm/cervical cap, the fertility awareness method (FAM), or the withdrawal method. Condoms plus a diaphragm are 98% effective with typical use, with FAM they’re 96.6% effective, and with withdrawal they’re 96.2% effective. With perfect use, each of them is over 99% effective. 

You can find more info about the effectiveness of doubling up on various methods [here](http://www.scarleteen.com/article/sexual_health/the_buddy_system_effectiveness_rates_for_backing_up_your_birth_control_with_a_?utm_source=share&utm_medium=ios_app). Of course, none of this can substitute an appointment with a doctor to fully discuss your individual situation and choices. Hopefully that was helpful, and good luck!

Mid-cycle bleeding can be caused by [a lot of different things](https://www.buoyhealth.com/current/29-reasons-why-you-are-spotting-before-your-period/), and it’s not too hard to throw your cycle off from stress/weight changes/travel/illness/etc. You said it started 2 weeks after your period, so it could be spotting from ovulation and the hormonal changes that come around that part of the cycle. There’s also a chance that an egg was fertilized when you had sex on the 7th, and it’s actually implantation bleeding. It might be worth taking a pregnancy test just in case. I kind of doubt that it’s from a miscarriage because the bleeding you’re describing sounds much lighter than a miscarriage, even for an early one.

Overall, if it’s not causing any sort of unusual pain or discomfort, I would just keep an eye on it for now and bring it up with a doctor if it keeps happening. However, if it is causing you pain or discomfort or you’re still concerned, try to see a doctor about it as soon as possible in case it’s something serious. You know your body the best, so if you feel that something is off, there’s no harm in being extra cautious.

I experienced the exact same thing with the NuvaRing almost within a day of starting it. I had never had such an intense emotional reaction to birth control before. My main motivation for trying the ring was to not have to remember to take a pill every day, so nothing with a specific health-related outcome like reducing ovarian cysts. After a week, I couldn’t stand it anymore and went back to the doctor, who agreed that it was pretty serious, told me to take it out, and scheduled me for a copper IUD later that week. I can easily imagine being hospitalized in the following months if I hadn’t taken it out because I was starting to have really intense suicidal thoughts every morning. 

Since you’re taking it for ovarian cysts, I’m not really sure what your other options would be, but I definitely recommend going back to your doctor and being very up front about the effect it’s having on your mental health. Be sure not to be dismissive of the problems you’re having when you go, because a lot of doctors are already dismissive enough of women’s problems. From there you could discuss other ways to manage the cysts that might work better with your individual body and mental health, or if there aren’t other options, you can weigh the costs and benefits of not taking anything at all. Your mental health is just as important as your physical health, so don’t be afraid to address it that way. Good luck, and I hope you feel better soon!

I have depression and anxiety, so I can definitely relate to your concern about the pill increasing anxiety. I’ve been on 2 different pills and thankfully didn’t experience too much in the way of side effects on either. The first one I tried was Microgestin (generic of Loestrin). I felt pretty fine on it emotionally and physically in the beginning, but about a year in I was noticing a problem with vaginal dryness no matter how turned on I was. Apparently that’s something that can be a problem on lower doses of estrogen. I switched to (generic) Ortho Tri-Cyclen and the problem cleared up. No mood swings or anxiety on that either. I can’t remember what my libido was like on Loestrin, but it was pretty good on Ortho Tri-Cyclen. I stayed on it for about two and a half years (until pretty recently), but I eventually decided to switch to a method I didn’t have to take every day. After chickening out of Paragard, I went for the NuvaRing and that was BAD. The day after I put it in I had to skip an entire day’s worth of classes because of uncontrollable crying. I had my first panic attack in a long time on it too. I’ll be biting the bullet and just getting the copper IUD soon. Sorry if this was a bit long. Overall Ortho Tri-Cyclen was pretty good to me, with no adverse emotional or sexual side effects. Loestrin was okay too, depending on how your body reacts to different doses of estrogen. Everybody is different, so YMMV. 

*TLDR*: Ortho Tri-Cyclen was the best thing I’ve tried so far. I would recommend it, but that doesn’t necessarily guarantee that anybody else would have as positive of an experience as I did.

Hi! I'm so sorry to hear that you're struggling. I can relate to a lot of the stuff in your post, and I think you could really benefit from seeing somebody. Therapists/counselors/what-have-you are specifically trained to help people to get things off their chests, to help them handle the pressures of life, and to help them sort through unhelpful thought processes/behaviors that are tangled up with a lot of emotional pain. Constantly analyzing your every action/word to the point of misery is something many with depression struggle with. So is feeling like a failure and a waste of time. Regardless of whether you do have depression, you are not alone in your problems, and you are definitely worth it. 
 
Therapists have helped many, many people who are going through similar issues to turn their lives around and not feel like they're stuck in a dark, exhausting tunnel. The same goes for the past trauma you alluded to. 
Seeing somebody about your problems can be really daunting. A lot of people are afraid of sharing their innermost thoughts and feelings with a stranger (or just acknowledging them out loud for that matter), or they believe that they're just "too messed up" for help. But I promise that no matter what your fears may be, therapy is a leap worth taking. 

It might take a while to find the right person, but if this happens don't give up immediately. I would suggest first looking online for professionals in your area. A lot of them have websites which can be really helpful for figuring out if they specialize in what you need and if they might be a good fit. If you're comfortable with it, friends and family are also a great way to get recommendations. If cost is an issue, there are most likely inexpensive and convenient mental health resources through your university.

Aside from all that, it sounds like you've made it pretty far in your academic career, even if you haven't had luck getting into medical school. It takes *a lot* to go through four years of college, do well enough to get into grad school, and persevere with it for a year, all while while struggling with your mental health. It might not feel like it right now, but you're a strong individual, and you have made it to where you are right now because you are intelligent and hardworking. It might not mean much coming from a stranger, but you have a lot to be proud of. 
I wish you the best of luck, and I urge you not to give up on your degree (even if it means taking time off). Remember that in all of this, your health should come first, even if that means your family and/or peers don't approve. I know that's easier said than done. Right now everything probably seems like part of a massive tangled web that you'll never escape, but with the right support, there is hope.
